{{Network science}}

'''Maximum-entropy random graph models''' are [[random graph]] models used to study [[complex networks]] subject to the [[principle of maximum entropy]] under a set of structural constraints,<ref name="Park">{{cite news
|title=The statistical mechanics of networks
|last=Park
|first=Juyong
|author2=M.E.J. Newman
|date=2004-05-25
|arxiv = cond-mat/0405566}}</ref> which may be global, distributional, or local.

==Overview==
Any random graph model (at a fixed set of parameter values) results in a [[probability distribution]] on [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]]s, and those that are maximum [[entropy]] within the considered class of distributions have the special property of being maximally [[unbiased]] [[null model]]s for network inference<ref name="van der Hoorn">{{cite news
|title=Sparse Maximum-Entropy Random Graphs with a Given Power-Law Degree Distribution
|last=van der Hoorn
|first=Pim
|author2=Gabor Lippner
|author3=Dmitri Krioukov
|date=2017-10-10
|arxiv = 1705.10261}}</ref> (e.g. [[biological network inference]]). Each model defines a family of probability distributions on the set of graphs of size <math>n</math> (for each <math>n>n_0</math> for some finite <math>n_0</math>), parameterized by a collection of constraints on <math>J</math> observables <math>\{Q_j(G)\}_{j=1}^J</math> defined for each graph <math>G</math> (such as fixed expected average [[degree (graph theory)|degree]], [[degree distribution]] of a particular form, or specific [[Degree (graph theory)#Degree sequence|degree sequence]]), enforced in the graph distribution alongside entropy maximization by the [[method of Lagrange multipliers]]. Note that in this context "maximum entropy" refers not to the [[graph entropy|entropy of a single graph]], but rather the entropy of the whole probabilistic ensemble of random graphs.

Several commonly studied random network models are in fact maximum entropy, for example the [[Erdos-Renyi model|ER]] graphs <math>G(n,m)</math> and <math>G(n,p)</math> (which each have one global constraint on the number of edges), as well as the [[configuration model]] (CM).<ref name="Newman 2010">{{cite book|title=Networks: An Introduction - Oxford Scholarship|last=Newman|first=Mark|doi=10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199206650.001.0001|year=2010|isbn=978-0-19-920665-0|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1281254|access-date=2018-09-13|archive-date=2023-02-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230204160415/https://catalogue.library.cern/legacy/1281254|url-status=live}}</ref> and [[soft configuration model]] (SCM) (which each have <math>n</math> local constraints, one for each nodewise degree-value). In the two pairs of models mentioned above, an important distinction<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Garlaschelli|first1=Diego|last2=den Hollander|first2=Frank|last3=Roccaverde|first3=Andrea|date=2018-07-13|title=Covariance Structure Behind Breaking of Ensemble Equivalence in Random Graphs|journal=Journal of Statistical Physics|volume=173|issue=3–4|pages=644–662|doi=10.1007/s10955-018-2114-x|issn=0022-4715|arxiv=1711.04273|bibcode=2018JSP...173..644G}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Roccaverde|first=Andrea|date=August 2018|title=Is breaking of ensemble equivalence monotone in the number of constraints?|journal=Indagationes Mathematicae|volume=30|pages=7–25|doi=10.1016/j.indag.2018.08.001|issn=0019-3577|arxiv=1807.02791}}</ref> is in whether the constraint is sharp (i.e. satisfied by every element of the set of size-<math>n</math> graphs with nonzero probability in the ensemble), or soft (i.e. satisfied on average across the whole ensemble). The former (sharp) case corresponds to a [[microcanonical ensemble]],<ref>{{cite book
 |last         = Bianconi
 |first        = G.
 |author-link  = Ginestra Bianconi
 |date         = 2018-08-21
 |title        = Multilayer Networks: Structure and Function
 |url          = https://global.oup.com/academic/product/multilayer-networks-9780198753919?cc=us&lang=en&
 |publisher    = Oxford University Press
 |isbn         = 978-0-19-875391-9
 |access-date  = 2018-09-13
 |archive-date = 2023-02-04
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20230204160403/https://global.oup.com/academic/product/multilayer-networks-9780198753919?cc=us&lang=en&
 |url-status   = live
}}</ref> the condition of maximum entropy yielding all graphs <math>G</math> satisfying <math>Q_j(G)=q_j\forall j</math> as equiprobable; the latter (soft) case is [[canonical ensemble|canonical]],<ref name="Anand">{{cite journal 
|last1=Anand
|first1=K. 
|last2=Bianconi
|first2=G. |author2-link= Ginestra Bianconi
|year=2009
|title=Entropy measures for networks: Toward an information theory of complex topologies
|journal=Physical Review E
|volume=80 
|issue=4 
|article-number=045102 
|doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.80.045102 
|pmid=19905379 
|arxiv=0907.1514 
|bibcode=2009PhRvE..80d5102A 
}}</ref> producing an [[exponential random graph model]] (ERGM).

|}

==Canonical ensemble of graphs (general framework)==
Suppose we are building a random graph model consisting of a probability distribution <math>\mathbb{P}(G)</math> on the set <math>\mathcal{G}_n</math> of [[simple graph]]s with <math>n</math> vertices. The  [[Entropy (statistical thermodynamics)#Gibbs entropy formula|Gibbs entropy]] <math>S[G]</math> of this ensemble will be given by

:      <math> S[G]=-\sum_{G\in \mathcal{G}_n}\mathbb{P}(G)\log\mathbb{P}(G).</math>

We would like the ensemble-averaged values <math>\{\langle Q_j \rangle\}_{j=1}^J</math> of observables <math>\{Q_j(G)\}_{j=1}^J</math> (such as average [[Degree (graph theory)|degree]], average [[Clustering coefficient|clustering]], or [[Average path length|average shortest path length]]) to be tunable, so we impose <math>J</math> "soft" constraints on the graph distribution:

:      <math> \langle Q_j \rangle = \sum_{G\in \mathcal{G}_n}\mathbb{P}(G)Q_j(G) = q_j, </math>

where <math>j=1,...,J</math> label the constraints. Application of the method of Lagrange multipliers to determine the distribution <math>\mathbb{P}(G)</math> that maximizes <math>S[G]</math> while satisfying <math>\langle Q_j \rangle=q_j</math>, and the normalization condition <math>\sum_{G\in \mathcal{G}_n}\mathbb{P}(G)=1</math> results in the following:<ref name="Park" />

:      <math> \mathbb{P}(G) = \frac{1}{Z}\exp\left[-\sum_{j=1}^J\psi_j Q_j(G)\right],</math>

where <math>Z</math> is a normalizing constant (the [[Partition function (mathematics)|partition function]]) and <math>\{\psi_j\}_{j=1}^J</math> are parameters (Lagrange multipliers) coupled to the correspondingly indexed graph observables, which may be tuned to yield graph samples with desired values of those properties, on average; the result is an exponential family and [[canonical ensemble]]; specifically yielding an [[exponential random graph model|ERGM]].

==The Erdős–Rényi model <math>G(n,m)</math>==

In the canonical framework above, constraints were imposed on ensemble-averaged quantities <math>\langle Q_j \rangle</math>. Although these properties will on average take on values specifiable by appropriate setting of <math>\{\psi_j\}_{j=1}^J</math>, each specific instance <math>G</math> may have <math>Q_j(G)\ne q_j</math>, which may be undesirable. Instead, we may impose a much stricter condition: every graph with nonzero probability must satisfy <math>Q_j(G)= q_j</math> exactly. Under these "sharp" constraints, the maximum-entropy distribution is determined. We exemplify this with the Erdős–Rényi model <math>G(n,m)</math>.

The sharp constraint in <math>G(n,m)</math> is that of a fixed number of [[Glossary of graph theory terms#edge|edges]] <math>m</math>,<ref name="ER">{{cite journal 
|last1=Erdős 
|first1=P. 
|last2=Rényi 
|first2=A. 
|year=2022 
|title=On Random Graphs. I 
|journal=  Publicationes Mathematicae Debrecen
|volume=6 
|issue=3–4 
|pages=290–297 
|doi=10.5486/PMD.1959.6.3-4.12 
|url=http://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1959-11.pdf 
|access-date=2018-09-13 
|archive-date=2020-08-07 
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200807021117/https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1959-11.pdf 
|url-status=live 
}}</ref> that is <math>|\operatorname E(G)|=m</math>, for all graphs <math>G</math> drawn from the ensemble (instantiated with a probability denoted <math>\mathbb{P}_{n,m}(G)</math>). This restricts the sample space from <math>\mathcal{G}_n</math> (all graphs on <math>n</math> vertices) to the subset <math>\mathcal{G}_{n,m}=\{g\in\mathcal{G}_n;|\operatorname E(g)|=m\}\subset \mathcal{G}_n</math>. This is in direct analogy to the [[microcanonical ensemble]] in classical [[statistical mechanics]], wherein the system is restricted to a thin manifold in the [[phase space]] of all states of a particular [[energy]] value.

Upon restricting our sample space to <math>\mathcal{G}_{n,m}</math>, we have no external constraints (besides normalization) to satisfy, and thus we'll select <math>\mathbb{P}_{n,m}(G)</math> to maximize <math>S[G]</math> without making use of Lagrange multipliers. It is well known that the entropy-maximizing distribution in the absence of external constraints is the [[Discrete uniform distribution|uniform distribution]] over the sample space (see [[maximum entropy probability distribution]]), from which we obtain:

:      <math>\mathbb{P}_{n,m}(G)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}_{n,m}|}=\binom{\binom{n}{2}}{m}^{-1},</math>

where the last expression in terms of [[binomial coefficients]] is the number of ways to place <math>m</math> edges among <math>\binom{n}{2}</math> possible [[Edge (graph theory)|edges]], and thus is the [[cardinality]] of <math>\mathcal{G}_{n,m}</math>.

==Generalizations==
A variety of maximum-entropy ensembles have been studied on generalizations of simple graphs. These include, for example, ensembles of simplicial complexes,<ref name="Zuev">{{cite news
|title=Exponential Random Simplicial Complexes
|last=Zuev
|first=Konstantin
|author2=Or Eisenberg
|author3=Dmitri Krioukov
|date=2015-10-29
|arxiv = 1502.05032}}
</ref> and weighted random graphs with a given expected degree sequence 
<ref name="Hillar">{{cite news
|title=Maximum entropy distributions on graphs
|last=Hillar
|first=Christopher
|author2=Andre Wibisono
|date=2013-08-26
|arxiv = 1301.3321}}
</ref>
